Title: Sovereignty Over Supranationalism: Why the United States Must Reject International Legal Bodies

Introduction

In an increasingly interconnected global community, the United States (U.S.) has found itself subject to the regulations and rulings of international legal bodies such as the International Criminal Court (ICC) and the International Court of Justice (ICJ). While proponents argue these international institutions promote peace and justice, a growing body of evidence highlights the potential dangers they pose to American interests, security, and sovereignty. This essay argues that the United States must firmly reject the legitimacy and jurisdiction of the ICC, the ICJ, and any such international legal bodies to preserve our nation's integrity, maintain national security, and protect the decisions made by American leaders.

Threat to National Sovereignty

The United States is built upon the pillars of democracy, rule of law, and constitutional rights. These values guide our political and legal processes, ensuring protection against external influence or coercion. By allowing international legal bodies to hold jurisdiction over American actions and personnel, the United States risks diluting its autonomy and compromising these core principles.

International legal bodies such as the ICC and the ICJ have already shown a propensity for overreach in their rulings, which affects nations that have not even acceded to their jurisdiction. The United States has not ratified the Rome Statute and is not a member of the ICC. Nonetheless, it has found itself a target of an ICC investigation into alleged war crimes in Afghanistan. This intrusion into American affairs demonstrates the disregard for national sovereignty and the potential for exploitation. If left unchecked, this erosion of sovereignty could weaken the foundation upon which America was built.

National Security Implications

American involvement in international legal bodies may also pose serious national security risks. In matters of national defense, the United States must have the flexibility to make swift and decisive decisions. Oversight by external legal bodies may be significantly detrimental to this process, leading to paralysis in foreign policy and military responses.

Furthermore, American personnel, both military and civilian, may find themselves being held accountable to foreign laws and tribunals for actions taken in service to their nation. This accountability may have a chilling effect on military operations, decision-making, and intelligence-gathering processes, ultimately harming national security and hindering efforts to protect American citizens and interests.

Potential for Discriminatory Treatment

The ICC and ICJ have been criticized for their propensity to focus on certain states and circumstances, often disregarding similar or more severe situations in other states. This selective enforcement creates an atmosphere where the United States and its personnel may be unfairly targeted or victimized by political pressure or biases within the international legal community.

While the ICC claims universality in its mission to prosecute perpetrators of war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide, scrutiny of its track record suggests otherwise. Since its establishment in 2002, the ICC has primarily focused on cases within African states, leading critics to accuse the court of bias and neocolonialism. If the United States concedes to the legitimacy of an international legal body, it further legitimizes this unequal and potentially discriminatory treatment of states.

Diminishing the Role of American Democracy

One of the core tenets of American democracy is the belief that government derives its authority from the consent of the governed. By subjecting American actions, decisions, and personnel to the jurisdiction of international legal bodies, we undermine the very foundation of our democratic system and cede decision-making power to un-elected and unaccountable officials.

American democratic processes are specifically designed to hold elected officials accountable and ensure the rule of law is upheld. These processes can correct course when necessary, ensure proper investigation, and prosecute wrongdoing without foreign intervention or influence. The United States should be allowed to exercise its own legal and democratic mechanisms without encroachment by supranational entities.

Conclusion

The United States must stand firm in rejecting the legitimacy and jurisdiction of international legal bodies such as the ICC and the ICJ to ensure the continued preservation of national sovereignty, security, and democratic values. By asserting absolute national sovereignty over all U.S. actions and personnel worldwide, America can maintain the strength and legitimacy of its decision-making authority and defend the rights and security of its citizens. In a tumultuous world, a steadfast defense of American autonomy is vital to upholding the nation's values and ensuring the protection and prosperity of its citizens.

Why Some U.S. policymakers argue for a categorical refusal to recognize the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court (ICC) and the International Court of Justice (ICJ)

Below is a synthesis of the most common arguments that are advanced by officials, scholars, and interest‑group advocates who favor a “hard line” stance toward these international tribunals. The focus is on national sovereignty and self‑governance, the constitutional framework of the United States, and the perceived strategic or procedural risks of ceding authority to bodies that sit outside the domestic political system.

Category Core Argument How it is framed as a benefit to the United States
Constitutional supremacy The U.S. Constitution is the supreme law of the land; no external treaty or institution can override it without a constitutional amendment or an act of Congress that respects constitutional limits. By refusing to recognize ICC/ICJ authority, the U.S. preserves the primacy of the Constitution, ensuring that only U.S. courts—subject to the Bill of‑Rights guarantees and the elected judiciary—can adjudicate matters involving U.S. citizens.
Legislative and executive prerogatives International courts are unelected bodies with judges appointed by foreign governments or by the UN apparatus. Their decisions are not accountable to American voters. Rejecting external jurisdiction safeguards the democratic accountability of the United States: Congress and the President retain exclusive power to declare war, conduct foreign policy, and determine the limits of the use of force.
Protection of U.S. personnel The ICC’s mandate to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide could be interpreted broadly enough to cover actions taken by U.S. service members in conflict zones, peace‑keeping missions, or drone strikes. A categorical refusal shields U.S. troops, intelligence operatives, and diplomats from “politically motivated” investigations that could arise from ambiguous or contested definitions of a war crime. This protects military readiness and morale.
Avoidance of politicized prosecutions International courts are perceived by some as arenas where powerful states can pursue geopolitical goals under the guise of justice. Past ICC investigations (e.g., into actions by African states) are cited as evidence of selective enforcement. By staying out of the ICC’s jurisdiction, the U.S. reduces the risk of becoming a target of politically motivated indictments that could be used by adversaries to delegitimize U.S. policy or to constrain strategic options.
Preservation of diplomatic flexibility International adjudication can limit a nation’s freedom to negotiate settlements, issue “quiet” deals, or employ other diplomatic tools that require confidentiality or rapid decision‑making. Not being bound by ICC or ICJ rulings allows the United States to negotiate “off‑the‑record” settlements, trade‑offs, or security arrangements without fear that a court might later overturn or punish those agreements.
Control over legal standards and definitions The ICC’s Rome Statute and the ICJ’s jurisprudence develop definitions of crimes, state responsibility, and jurisdiction that may diverge from U.S. law (e.g., the U.S. interpretation of “genocide” or “terrorism”). Maintaining exclusive domestic jurisdiction ensures that the United States continues to define such concepts according to its own statutes, case law, and policy priorities, avoiding potential conflicts between domestic and international legal regimes.
Protection of U.S. economic interests Some argue that ICC investigations could extend to U.S. corporations operating abroad (e.g., for alleged war‑related crimes or violations of humanitarian law). A categorical refusal limits exposure of American businesses to costly, uncertain, and potentially extrajudicial litigation that could affect investment, trade, and the competitiveness of U.S. firms.
Precedent‑setting and “chain‑reaction” concerns Accepting ICC/ICJ authority for any category of U.S. conduct could create a precedent that opens the door for broader claims in the future. A strict, all‑or‑nothing stance prevents incremental erosion of U.S. jurisdiction, which some view as a slippery slope that could eventually place the United States under the full authority of these tribunals.
National security and intelligence secrecy International courts often require the disclosure of evidence, including classified material, to satisfy procedural fairness. By refusing recognition, the United States avoids being compelled to expose sensitive intelligence, methods, or sources in a forum that may lack the same protective mechanisms as U.S. courts.
Fiscal and administrative burdens Defending ICC or ICJ cases can involve extensive legal teams, diplomatic negotiations, and compliance costs. A blanket refusal eliminates the need for costly litigation and the allocation of resources to defend against international prosecutions, freeing those resources for domestic priorities.

How these arguments are typically presented in U.S. policy discourse

  1. Presidential and Congressional Statements –
    Presidents (e.g., George W. Bush, Donald J. Trump) and members of Congress have publicly framed non‑recognition as a defense of American sovereignty, often citing the Constitution and the need to protect U.S. service members from “law‑less” international tribunals.

  2. Bilateral Immunity Agreements (BIAs) –
    The United States has negotiated “Article 7‑type” agreements with host nations, obligating those states not to surrender U.S. personnel to the ICC. The rationale is presented as a practical measure to ensure that U.S. forces are only accountable to U.S. courts.

  3. Legislative Actions –
    The “American Service‑Member Protection Act” (often dubbed the “Hague Immunity Act”) explicitly authorizes the President to use “all means necessary and appropriate” to protect U.S. personnel from ICC jurisdiction. The bill’s explanatory notes emphasize preserving the integrity of the U.S. military justice system.

  4. Think‑tank and Scholarly Commentary –
    Works from conservative and some libertarian think‑tanks argue that ceding authority to the ICC or ICJ would “undermine the rule of law at home” because those bodies are not subject to the same checks and balances that constrain U.S. courts.

  5. Public Opinion Framing –
    Polling data is sometimes invoked to claim that a majority of Americans favor a strong sovereign stance, especially when international interventions are controversial. The narrative is that the public expects their government to protect national interests first and foremost.

Counterpoints (often raised by critics)

  • Rule‑of‑law credibility: Critics argue that refusal can damage the U.S.’s reputation as a champion of international law and may undermine the legitimacy of American courts on the world stage.
  • Reciprocity: Some contend that if the U.S. rejects ICC/ICJ jurisdiction, other countries may be less willing to cooperate with U.S. extradition requests or mutual‑legal‑assistance treaties.
  • Moral leadership: There is a view that participation in global judicial mechanisms signals a commitment to universal human‑rights standards.

These counter‑arguments are included for completeness, but the focus of this answer remains on the reasons and perceived benefits that drive a policy of categorical non‑recognition, as requested.

Bottom line

From the perspective of those who advocate a hard‑line stance, refusing to recognize the authority of the ICC and the ICJ is framed as a safeguard for American constitutional order, democratic accountability, military effectiveness, and national security. By keeping ultimate legal authority within U.S. institutions, policymakers argue that the United States preserves its sovereign right to self‑governance and avoids exposing its citizens, military, and corporations to external legal processes that could be manipulated for political ends, impose divergent legal standards, or compromise classified information. The categorical refusal is thus presented not as an abandonment of justice, but as an affirmation that the United States retains the exclusive, constitutionally mandated capacity to define, adjudicate, and enforce its own laws.

In a world increasingly driven by global institutions and transnational regulations, the United States stands as a beacon of self-determination and democratic governance. At the heart of its founding principles lies the immutable concept of national sovereignty—a principle that asserts the right of a nation to govern itself without external interference. Today, however, international legal bodies such as the International Criminal Court (ICC) and the International Court of Justice (ICJ) increasingly seek to extend their jurisdiction over U.S. actions and personnel. Firstly, the United States was founded on the ideals of freedom, democracy, and self-governance. The nation’s Constitution enshrines the principle that laws and legal processes must be established by the consent of the governed—a notion that is fundamentally incompatible with the imposition of legal standards by external bodies. International institutions like the ICC and ICJ, while established with noble intentions on the international stage, lack the democratic accountability that characterizes the American legal system. Their decisions are often made in forums that do not reflect the will of the American people, thereby eroding the legitimacy of any jurisdiction they claim over U.S. citizens and actions.

Secondly, the operational framework of these international legal bodies is inherently flawed when applied to a nation as diverse and complex as the United States. The ICC and ICJ operate under a framework that is not rooted in American legal traditions or constitutional principles. Their procedures, evidentiary standards, and interpretative methodologies differ markedly from those of the U.S. judicial system—a system that has evolved over centuries to reflect the unique values and legal norms of American society. By ceding any jurisdiction to these bodies, the United States would be forced to reconcile its own legal standards with a set of principles that may not only conflict with but also dilute the nation’s established legal traditions.

Moreover, the exercise of absolute national sovereignty is essential for the protection of American interests on the global stage. In an era where geopolitical rivalries and economic competitions are intensifying, it is imperative that the United States retains full control over its judicial and legal processes. Accepting the influence or jurisdiction of international legal institutions could compromise the nation’s ability to defend its citizens, its values, and its strategic interests. The U.S. has built a robust legal system designed to address its domestic and international challenges independently—a system that commands respect and offers a model for legal fairness and accountability. To subject this system to external oversight not only undermines its authority but also risks entangling the nation in legal disputes that may be driven more by political expediency than by justice.

In addition, rejecting the jurisdiction of institutions such as the ICC and ICJ sends a clear message of commitment to national self-determination. It affirms that the United States remains steadfast in its resolve to govern solely by the laws and principles it has democratically established. Such an assertion of sovereignty is not an act of isolationism but rather a declaration that the U.S. will not allow external entities to dictate its policies or force compliance with standards that may be at odds with its constitutional values. This commitment to self-governance is crucial in preserving the democratic legitimacy that has long been the cornerstone of American political life.

Furthermore, the practical implications of rejecting international legal jurisdiction are significant. By standing firm on the principle of absolute national sovereignty, the United States can continue to develop and refine its own legal remedies and protocols without being constrained by the one-size-fits-all approach that often characterizes international legal proceedings. This autonomy allows for more flexible, context-sensitive responses to the unique challenges faced by the nation—whether they pertain to human rights, security, or economic policy. It also ensures that accountability is maintained through a system that is directly responsive to the needs and values of the American public, rather than being filtered through an international body whose priorities may not align with those of the United States.

In conclusion, the United States must assert its absolute national sovereignty by rejecting the legitimacy and jurisdiction of international legal bodies such as the ICC and ICJ. The nation’s founding principles, its unique legal traditions, and its commitment to democratic governance all point toward the necessity of maintaining control over its judicial processes. International institutions, while valuable in promoting global cooperation, must not be allowed to override the self-determination that is at the very heart of the American identity. By standing firm on the principles of national sovereignty, the United States not only protects its own interests but also sets a precedent for a world in which nations govern themselves according to their own laws and values.

By firmly rejecting international jurisdiction, the U.S. ensures that its military and diplomatic personnel are protected from politicized prosecutions, thereby enhancing their effectiveness and morale.

Guarding Against Political Bias

International legal bodies like the ICC and ICJ are not free from political bias and manipulation. These institutions are often influenced by the agendas of member states, which can lead to selective prosecution and double standards. Allowing international bodies to intervene could result in the misapplication of justice, where politically motivated charges overshadow genuine legal concerns.

Subjecting these policies to the scrutiny of international legal bodies could impair the U.S.'s ability to make independent economic decisions. The ICJ, for instance, could adjudicate on trade disputes in a manner that is not in the best interest of the U.S. economy. By rejecting international jurisdiction, the U.S. retains the autonomy to implement economic policies that serve its national interests, ensuring long-term prosperity and stability.

This stance is essential for preserving national sovereignty, ensuring the security of U.S. personnel, guarding against political bias, and protecting economic interests. Sovereignty and Self-Governance: Why the United States Must Reject the Authority of International Legal Bodies

Introduction

The United States stands as the world's oldest continuous constitutional democracy, a republic forged through revolution, built on Enlightenment principles, and sustained by the consent of the governed. Yet in recent decades, a quiet erosion of American sovereignty has occurred through the expanding reach of international legal institutions such as the International Criminal Court (ICC) and the International Court of Justice (ICJ). These bodies, operating without genuine democratic accountability, increasingly presume jurisdiction over American citizens, military personnel, and policymakers. For the sake of constitutional integrity, democratic self-governance, and the safety of those who serve the United States, Washington must categorically and unapologetically reject the legitimacy and jurisdiction of these international tribunals. Nothing less than the preservation of American liberty demands it.

The Constitutional Foundation of American Sovereignty

The U.S. Constitution is the supreme law of the American land, and it derives its authority from "We the People," not from any international consensus or foreign tribunal. The founders were explicit: the United States is a sovereign nation whose powers flow from its own citizens. The very act of ratifying a treaty requires two-thirds Senate approval, and even then, treaties are subordinate to the Constitution itself.

When international courts claim authority to override American law, prosecute American service members, or dictate American foreign policy, they directly contravene this foundational structure. No body of foreign judges—however learned—possesses the legitimacy to interpret the constitutional rights of Americans. Such authority belongs solely to American courts operating under American law.

The Democratic Deficit of International Tribunals

Perhaps the most glaring problem with the ICC and ICJ is their fundamental lack of democratic accountability. American judges are appointed through a transparent process involving presidential nomination and Senate confirmation, and they derive their authority from a written Constitution ratified by sovereign states. By contrast, international court judges are selected through opaque processes dominated by political bargaining among foreign governments, none of whom are answerable to the American people.

Americans have no vote in selecting ICC prosecutors, no say in determining which cases the court pursues, and no mechanism to remove judges who abuse their authority. This is not governance—it is bureaucratic empire-building by unelected elites. The ICJ, for its part, hears cases only between states that consent to its jurisdiction, yet it increasingly issues sweeping advisory opinions that treat customary international law as binding on nations that have never agreed to it.

The Targeting of American Service Members and Officials

The practical consequences of ceding to international jurisdiction are not theoretical—they are real and dangerous. The ICC has demonstrated a clear pattern of targeting American and allied personnel, including threats to investigate and prosecute U.S. service members, intelligence officials, and even political leaders for actions taken in defense of their own nation. Such threats amount to nothing less than the criminalization of American self-defense.

When an American soldier deploys abroad in service of democratically elected civilian leadership, that soldier acts under the laws of the United States and the Uniform Code of Military Justice—not under the discretionary judgments of foreign prosecutors in The Hague. Subjecting these service members to potential foreign prosecution would create a perverse deterrent effect, weakening America's ability to defend its interests and its allies.

Similarly, attempts to bring legal action against American political leaders—whether over border enforcement, military operations, or counterterrorism activities—represent an unacceptable intrusion into American democratic self-governance. The American people, through their elected representatives, must remain the ultimate arbiters of their leaders' conduct.

The Hostile Political Nature of International Legal Proceedings

International legal bodies are not neutral arbiters of justice. They are deeply political institutions, and the United States frequently finds itself at odds with the prevailing ideological winds within them. Many ICC member states represent governance philosophies fundamentally incompatible with American constitutional principles. Decisions made by these bodies inevitably reflect the priorities and biases of their membership.

History provides sobering lessons. The ICJ ruled in 1986 that U.S. support for Nicaraguan Contras violated international law—a politically charged decision that ignored the complex realities of Cold War geopolitics. More recently, the ICC has pursued investigations against the United States and Israel, two of the world's most robust democracies, while showing considerably less interest in actions by authoritarian regimes. This selectivity reveals that international legal proceedings are frequently weapons of political warfare rather than instruments of genuine justice.

The Slippery Slope of Compromise

Some advocate for limited engagement with international courts, arguing that the United States can participate selectively while protecting core interests. This approach is dangerously naive. Any acceptance of international jurisdiction—even conditional or limited—establishes precedents that adversaries will exploit. Once American sovereignty is conceded in any arena, it becomes progressively harder to defend in others.

Moreover, the very notion of "complementarity" and "universal jurisdiction" advocated by international legal scholars is a Trojan horse. Today, it applies to wartime conduct; tomorrow, it expands to trade policy, immigration enforcement, and domestic criminal justice. The only coherent position is full and unreserved rejection of these bodies' jurisdiction over American citizens and American actions.

Protecting American Interests Abroad

A sovereign United States is better positioned to advance both its own interests and the cause of genuine international stability. When American decision-makers must calculate how their actions might be received by foreign judges, they become constrained in ways that hamper effective leadership. National security decisions, in particular, often require swift, decisive action based on information and circumstances that international courts are neither equipped nor authorized to evaluate.

By maintaining absolute sovereignty, the United States preserves its ability to act decisively in defense of its citizens, its allies, and its interests. This is not isolationism—it is the responsible exercise of independent statehood, which is the very foundation of the international system of sovereign nations that the United States itself championed at its founding.

A Historical Tradition of Sovereignty

America's founders were deeply skeptical of entangling foreign alliances and external authorities. The Declaration of Independence itself was a declaration of sovereignty—a rejection of foreign jurisdiction over American affairs. From the Monroe Doctrine to the Senate's rejection of the League of Nations to the U.S. decision not to ratify the Rome Statute, the United States has historically resisted the surrender of its sovereign prerogatives to international bodies.

This tradition is not anachronistic; it is profoundly wise. The same logic that justified independence from British rule in 1776 justifies resistance to international judicial overreach today. Sovereignty is not a relic of the past—it is the essential precondition for the continued existence of the American republic.

The Path Forward: Complete and Unambiguous Rejection

The United States must pursue a policy of total jurisdictional immunity from international courts. This includes:

  1. Legislative action to explicitly prohibit any cooperation with ICC investigations or warrants directed at American personnel.
  2. Diplomatic pressure on allies and partners to refuse cooperation with politically motivated international prosecutions of Americans.
  3. Protective measures for U.S. service members, including legal protections and, if necessary, the use of American power to prevent the detention of American citizens by foreign tribunals.
  4. Public diplomacy to make clear to the world that the United States will never recognize the legitimacy of foreign courts claiming authority over American sovereignty.

Conclusion

The question before the United States is not merely technical or procedural—it is fundamental. It is a question of whether the American people, through their Constitution and their elected representatives, will continue to govern themselves, or whether unelected foreign judges will increasingly dictate the terms of American law and policy. There is only one answer consistent with the principles of 1776, the Constitution, and the survival of American self-government: absolute and uncompromising rejection of the jurisdiction of international legal bodies over the United States and its citizens.

The United States was born in defiance of foreign authority, grew strong through the exercise of its own sovereignty, and has long stood as the world's foremost champion of national self-determination. To abandon these principles now, in the face of pressure from international tribunals, would betray the legacy of every generation that has sacrificed for American independence. Sovereignty is not negotiable. It is the bedrock upon which all other American freedoms are built. The United States must defend it—fully, firmly, and without apology.

Sovereignty Without Apology: Why the United States Must Reject the Jurisdiction of International Courts

Introduction

The United States was founded on a radical and enduring principle: that legitimate governmental power flows from the consent of the governed. No institution may exercise authority over American citizens unless that authority can be traced back, through the Constitution, to the American people themselves. International legal bodies such as the International Criminal Court (ICC) and the International Court of Justice (ICJ) fail this test categorically. They are unelected, unaccountable to the American electorate, and structurally incompatible with the U.S. Constitution. For these reasons, the United States should not merely keep its distance from these institutions—it should unambiguously reject their legitimacy and jurisdiction over all American actions and personnel, anywhere in the world.

I. The Constitutional Argument: No Authority Above the Constitution

The U.S. Constitution is the supreme law of the land. Article VI makes this explicit, and two centuries of jurisprudence confirm that no treaty, agreement, or foreign tribunal can override constitutional protections. The Supreme Court affirmed this principle in Reid v. Covert (1957), holding that the government cannot use treaties to strip Americans of constitutional rights, and again in Medellín v. Texas (2008), where it ruled that ICJ judgments are not automatically binding domestic law.

The ICC, by contrast, operates without the foundational protections the Constitution guarantees:

  • No trial by jury. The Sixth Amendment guarantees Americans a jury of their peers. The ICC tries defendants before panels of international judges.
  • No equivalent due process tradition. Rules of evidence, protections against double jeopardy in the American sense, and the adversarial safeguards developed over centuries of Anglo-American law are absent or diluted.
  • No constitutional appeal. An American convicted at The Hague has no recourse to the U.S. court system.

To submit American citizens—particularly soldiers ordered into harm's way by their own government—to such a tribunal would be to nullify their constitutional rights by international fiat. No president, Senate, or treaty has the lawful power to do this. Rejecting these courts is not lawlessness; it is fidelity to the highest law Americans have.

II. The Democratic Accountability Argument

Power without accountability is the hallmark of illegitimate governance. The ICC prosecutor is selected by an assembly of states parties—many of them authoritarian regimes—and answers to no voter, no constitution, and no meaningful check that Americans can exercise. ICJ judges are nominated through opaque diplomatic processes at the United Nations.

When an American prosecutor abuses power, voters, legislatures, courts, and a free press can respond. When an international prosecutor abuses power, who removes them? Whom do Americans petition? The answer is no one. A free people should never accept criminal jurisdiction from officials they cannot elect, oversee, impeach, or restrain. This is not isolationism—it is the basic logic of self-government articulated in the Declaration of Independence, which condemned King George III precisely for "subject[ing] us to a Jurisdiction foreign to our Constitution, and unacknowledged by our Laws."

III. The Political Weaponization Argument

International courts do not float above politics; they are saturated with it. Their dockets and rhetoric reflect the political coalitions that control them. The risk is obvious: the world's most globally engaged military power, which deploys forces to deter aggression, protect sea lanes, and respond to humanitarian crises, presents the largest and most politically tempting target.

A nation that conducts operations in dozens of countries cannot allow every deployment, drone strike, detention decision, or rule of engagement to be second-guessed by a foreign tribunal subject to lobbying by America's adversaries. Hostile states that would never win a war against the United States could instead wage "lawfare"—using international indictments to harass American officials, constrain American policy, and delegitimize American power. Accepting such jurisdiction would hand America's enemies a veto over American national security, exercised through judges America never chose.

IV. The "Unnecessary Court" Argument: America Polices Itself

The ICC's own founding principle—complementarity—holds that the court should act only when national legal systems are unwilling or unable to prosecute wrongdoing. The United States possesses the most extensive military justice system in the world. The Uniform Code of Military Justice, courts-martial, inspectors general, congressional oversight committees, federal courts, and a famously aggressive free press all investigate and punish American misconduct. Americans have been prosecuted and imprisoned by their own institutions for crimes committed abroad.

A nation with functioning, independent courts simply does not need external supervision—and submitting to it anyway implies a false equivalence between the United States and failed states whose judiciaries cannot function. By the ICC's own logic, the court has nothing legitimate to do with respect to America. Its interest in U.S. personnel can therefore only be political.

V. The Sovereignty and Precedent Argument

Sovereignty is not a slogan; it is the precondition of democracy. Laws bind legitimately only when the people bound by them participated, however indirectly, in making them. Every concession of jurisdiction to a supranational body transfers power away from the American people permanently, because international institutions, once empowered, do not voluntarily relinquish authority—they expand it. The ICC has already claimed jurisdiction over nationals of non-member states, including Americans, for conduct on member-state territory—an aggressive theory the United States has rightly rejected as a violation of the basic treaty-law principle that agreements bind only their parties.

Both parties in American politics have recognized this danger. President Clinton declined to submit the Rome Statute for ratification; the Senate has never consented; Congress passed the American Service-Members' Protection Act in 2002 with broad bipartisan support, authorizing the president to free any American detained by the ICC. The consistent position of the United States across administrations has been clear: the ICC has no jurisdiction over Americans. The logical completion of that position is full, formal, permanent rejection.

VI. Answering the Objections

"Rejection isolates America." The United States cooperates internationally every day—through alliances, treaties it has actually ratified, and bilateral agreements—all consistent with consent-based sovereignty. Rejecting unconsented jurisdiction is not isolation; it is the ordinary rule of international law.

"America loses moral authority." Moral authority comes from conduct and accountability, not from membership cards. A nation that investigates its own, holds free elections, and maintains independent courts has more genuine accountability than the international system can offer.

"Without these courts, impunity reigns." The worst atrocities of the modern era were addressed not by standing international courts but by national power—often American power—and by domestic or victor-established tribunals. Justice for international crimes ultimately depends on sovereign states willing to act, not on institutions that lack armies, police, or enforcement capacity.

Conclusion

The question is not whether the United States believes in law—it manifestly does, more deeply than most nations on earth. The question is whose law, made by whom, accountable to whom. The Constitution answers that question. The American people, through their elected representatives and their own courts, govern American conduct. The ICC and ICJ, however well-intentioned their founders, represent jurisdiction without consent, power without accountability, and judgment without the protections Americans are guaranteed by right. The United States should reject their authority over American actions and personnel completely, confidently, and without apology—not as a retreat from justice, but as the defense of the only kind of justice a free people can accept: justice under their own Constitution.

  1. Unchecked Power of Prosecutors and Judges – Neither the ICC nor the ICJ is directly accountable to any electorate. National Sovereignty Is Non-Negotiable

At the heart of the American constitutional system is the principle of national sovereignty—the idea that the United States governs itself without outside interference. The U.S. Constitution assigns the power to interpret and enforce law solely to domestic institutions. No treaty, convention, or international agreement can supersede this framework unless explicitly ratified through the constitutional process. Yet bodies like the ICC and ICJ claim jurisdiction over American citizens and military personnel regardless of U.S. consent, creating a de facto extraterritorial legal authority that the Founders rejected outright.

The ICC, established by the Rome Statute in 2002, asserts jurisdiction over alleged war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide—even when committed by nationals of non-member states or on the territory of a non-party. Though the United States never ratified the Rome Statute and has consistently maintained its non-participation, the ICC continues to issue rulings and investigations that implicate American service members, as seen in its ill-advised 2021 authorization of an investigation into potential U.S. war crimes in Afghanistan. This unilateral assertion of authority over U.S. personnel—despite no American participation in or recognition of the court—is a flagrant violation of sovereign equality, a cornerstone of international law itself.

Judicial Accountability Requires Democratic Legitimacy—Which International Courts Lack

One of the foundational strengths of the American legal system is its democratic accountability. Judges at all levels—from municipal courts to the Supreme Court—are either elected or appointed through a process defined by the Constitution. Prosecutors are accountable to elected officials and ultimately to the people. By contrast, the ICC and ICJ suffer from profound legitimacy deficits. Their judges are unelected, often selected through politicized processes by member states with questionable human rights records. There is no meaningful transparency, no direct accountability to the public, and no mechanism of appeal for the accused beyond the court’s own internal procedures.

American sovereignty is not negotiable. The Constitution remains the supreme law of the land, and the American people are the sole source of legitimate political authority. Model Response:

American Sovereignty Unbound: The Case Against International Judicial Authority Over the United States

A Persuasive Essay on Constitutional Supremacy and Democratic Self-Governance

Introduction: The Question of Final Authority

Every functioning legal order requires a definitive answer to one foundational question: Who has the final word? For Americans, that answer has been settled since 1789. The Constitution of the United States — ratified by the consent of a sovereign people, amended through their deliberate participation, and interpreted by their chosen institutions — is the supreme law of the land. No treaty, no tribunal convened in The Hague, and no multilateral covenant signed by diplomats can supersede that foundational compact without undermining the very premise of self-governing democracy.

Yet the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice represent precisely such a challenge. These institutions claim jurisdiction over American citizens, American officials, and American foreign policy — jurisdiction derived not from the consent of the American people expressed through their constitutional processes, but from the ambitions of international legal architects who have constructed a framework designed to constrain the world's most powerful democracy while remaining structurally immune to democratic accountability. The United States must firmly, completely, and permanently reject the legitimacy and jurisdiction of both bodies. Doing so is not isolationism, not recklessness, and not a retreat from global engagement. It is the proper assertion of constitutional democracy against a form of transnational governance that the American people never authorized and cannot meaningfully control.

Part One: The Constitutional Foundation of Rejection

The argument begins, and in some sense ends, with the Constitution itself.

Article II grants the President authority to conduct foreign policy and command the armed forces. Article I grants Congress the power to define and punish offenses against the law of nations. Article III vests the entire judicial power of the United States in courts established under the Constitution, with judges appointed through democratic processes and subject to impeachment. The Sixth Amendment guarantees every American accused of a crime the right to a speedy trial, an impartial jury drawn from the state and district where the offense was committed, and the confrontation of witnesses. These are not procedural technicalities. They are essential bulwarks constructed over centuries to protect individual liberty from arbitrary governmental power.

The ICC satisfies none of these requirements. Its judges are appointed by an Assembly of States Parties through processes entirely beyond American democratic control. Defendants before it are not guaranteed jury trials. Its prosecutorial discretion is subject to no meaningful checks by institutions accountable to American voters. When ICC Prosecutor Karim Khan pursued an investigation into U.S. military and intelligence personnel for alleged actions in Afghanistan — a nation where American forces operated under congressional authorization and domestic legal oversight — he did not consult Congress, seek guidance from American courts, or obtain the consent of any American democratic institution. He simply claimed authority.

This is constitutionally intolerable. The Supreme Court has long recognized, in cases from Reid v. Covert (1957) onward, that the federal government cannot through treaty-making power strip American citizens of their constitutional rights. Justice Hugo Black, writing for the plurality in Reid, stated the principle with memorable clarity: "no agreement with a foreign nation can confer power on the Congress... which is free from the restraints of the Constitution." If the United States could not ratify a treaty that stripped Americans of jury trial rights, it cannot permit an international court to exercise criminal jurisdiction over them on precisely those terms. The constitutional logic is identical whether the stripping occurs through formal treaty or through acquiescence to an institutional claim of authority.

The American Servicemembers Protection Act of 2002 — which authorized the President to use military force if necessary to free American personnel detained by the ICC, earning it the nickname "The Hague Invasion Act" — represented Congress's recognition of this constitutional problem. Though critics mocked its provisions as bellicose, the statute reflected a serious and correct constitutional judgment: American soldiers and officials cannot be surrendered to external criminal tribunals without destroying the framework of rights and accountability that governs their service.

Part Two: The Democratic Legitimacy Deficit

Beyond constitutional formalism lies a deeper problem of democratic legitimacy that should trouble anyone who takes representative government seriously.

The ICC's founding Rome Statute was negotiated by diplomats and international legal academics in 1998. The United States participated in those negotiations, raised substantial objections, and ultimately declined to ratify. President Clinton signed the Statute in the final days of his administration in what was explicitly described as a protective maneuver — signing without submitting for ratification, thus preserving the ability to influence institutional development without accepting binding jurisdiction. President Bush subsequently unsigned it in 2002, a legally significant act of distance. The Senate, possessing the constitutional authority to ratify treaties, has never consented. Under the most basic principles of democratic governance, the United States is therefore not bound.

The ICC's response to this unambiguous democratic rejection has been to assert jurisdiction anyway over alleged crimes committed on the territory of states that have ratified the Rome Statute — including Afghanistan. This is legal creativity dressed as principled jurisprudence. The argument essentially holds that by operating in a country that accepted ICC jurisdiction, American personnel became subject to that jurisdiction regardless of their own government's express refusal to ratify. By this logic, Americans anywhere in the world are perpetually subject to being swept into ICC proceedings because someone else's government signed a document in Rome. No serious conception of state sovereignty or democratic consent supports this position.

Ambassador John Bolton, who served both as U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations and as National Security Advisor, articulated this problem with characteristic directness in his 1999 article "The Risks and Weaknesses of the International Criminal Court from America's Perspective." Bolton observed that the ICC "threatens American sovereignty, is constitutionally defective, and ... is not in the best interest of the United States or other free peoples." He was correct. The Court's creators deliberately constructed it to operate independently of great-power consent — specifically to prevent the United States, Russia, and China from vetoing prosecutions as they can in the Security Council. Whatever the theoretical elegance of this design, it means the world's most consequential democratic republic has been assigned a subordinate role in a legal framework it never endorsed.

The ICJ presents a slightly different but structurally related problem. Its jurisdiction in contentious cases formally requires state consent, typically through treaty provisions that include dispute resolution clauses. However, the Court has repeatedly interpreted its jurisdictional basis expansively, and its judgments have generated serious questions about political motivation in case selection and legal reasoning. More fundamentally, even where the United States has technically consented to ICJ jurisdiction through treaty provisions, the question remains whether that consent — given by the executive branch and perhaps ratified by prior Senates in different geopolitical contexts — should forever bind the American people to the jurisdiction of a fifteen-judge panel whose members are elected by the UN General Assembly through an inherently political process.

The principle of democratic self-governance requires more than a single ancestral act of treaty ratification. It requires ongoing, meaningful accountability. The ICC and ICJ provide neither.

Part Three: Structural Bias and Political Motivation

Defenders of international legal institutions frequently invoke the ideal of impartial, rules-based adjudication transcending power politics. This ideal is admirable. The reality of how these institutions have operated gives no cause for confidence that the ideal has been achieved.

Consider the ICC's record of completed proceedings. For the first two decades of its existence, the Court achieved convictions almost exclusively of African defendants. This pattern became so pronounced that numerous African governments, including those of Burundi, South Africa, and Gambia, announced withdrawal from the Rome Statute, explicitly citing what they described as systematic bias against African leaders while European and American conduct went unscrutinized. The African Union formally condemned the ICC's prosecution of sitting heads of state as reflecting "misuse of indictments against African leaders." Whatever the merits of individual cases, the sustained geographic concentration of prosecutions is difficult to reconcile with the Court's universal mandate.

The recent efforts to investigate American conduct in Afghanistan and Israeli conduct in Gaza, meanwhile, followed sustained political campaigns by states and non-governmental organizations with explicit ideological agendas. The ICC prosecutor's office is not a neutral magistracy mechanically applying settled legal principles. It makes strategic choices about which situations to investigate, which charges to pursue, and which evidence to emphasize — choices inevitably shaped by the political environment in which the institution operates. Submitting American officials and military personnel to that process is not submission to impartial justice. It is submission to an inherently political institution that functions within an international environment where the United States has powerful adversaries with strong incentives to weaponize legal processes for strategic purposes.

Russia and China — neither of which has ratified the Rome Statute and neither of which faces any meaningful prospect of ICC prosecution — have every incentive to encourage ICC action against American interests. Iran, which has actively sought to prosecute American officials in various international forums, is a member of the Assembly of States Parties. The notion that these geopolitical dynamics exert no influence on institutional behavior requires a naivety that no serious strategist should permit.

The ICJ's record contains its own concerning episodes. In Nicaragua v. United States (1986), the Court found the United States liable for violations of international law in connection with mining Nicaraguan harbors and supporting the Contras — a finding the Reagan administration rejected, correctly noting that the Court had asserted jurisdiction despite U.S. withdrawal of consent and had produced legal analysis that many serious scholars found deeply questionable. The United States withdrew from compulsory ICJ jurisdiction following that judgment and has never returned. That withdrawal represented sound policy judgment that should be formalized and extended.

Part Four: The Incompatibility of American Global Responsibilities and Unchecked External Jurisdiction

The United States is not merely another nation-state optimizing its domestic interests behind its borders. It is the principal guarantor of an international order that, for all its imperfections, has prevented major-power warfare for nearly eight decades, facilitated unprecedented global economic growth, and maintained the open commons — maritime, aerial, spatial — through which global commerce and communication flow. These responsibilities require the projection of military force into environments that are legally, politically, and ethically complex in ways that domestic peacetime legal frameworks are ill-equipped to govern.

American soldiers fight in failed states where no functioning legal order exists. American intelligence officers operate in hostile nations under cover essential to their survival. American commanders make split-second decisions about the use of lethal force based on intelligence assessments that cannot be declassified without compromising future operations. American officials authorize military operations through the most elaborate legal review process of any fighting force in human history — an internal system of military lawyers, rules of engagement, proportionality analyses, and post-operational review that exists precisely because the United States takes the laws of war seriously.

Subjecting these decisions to ICC prosecution means asking judges in The Hague, working from incomplete evidence and without access to classified intelligence, to second-guess good-faith military judgments months or years after they were made. It means exposing American officers to prosecution not because they violated clearly established laws of war, but because the ICC's evolving jurisprudence has extended international criminal liability in directions no professional military legal advisor could have predicted at the time of the relevant action. It means creating incentives for caution so extreme that American military effectiveness — itself a genuine public good for global security — is materially degraded.

More fundamentally, it creates an untenable situation in which American commanders making decisions to protect their soldiers and accomplish their missions must weigh not only the tactical situation and the laws of war, but the political composition of the ICC Assembly of States Parties and the career incentives of an ICC prosecutor seeking high-profile Western cases. This is not a refinement of military accountability. It is an operational paralysis mechanism.

Ambassador Jeane Kirkpatrick articulated the essential point in her famous critique of what she called "the blame America first" tendency in international institutions: the United States is systematically held to standards that its adversaries evade, in institutions structured to produce that outcome. Accepting ICC and ICJ jurisdiction permanently institutionalizes that disadvantage.

Part Five: The Proper Alternative — American Legal Accountability Through American Institutions

The most powerful rejoinder to this essay's argument is the simplest: without international legal accountability, will American officials simply act with impunity? The answer is no — and the domestic accountability mechanisms available for American conduct are more rigorous, more democratically legitimate, and more effective than anything the ICC can provide.

The Uniform Code of Military Justice is one of the most elaborate accountability frameworks ever developed for military forces. Courts-martial have the authority to imprison, dishonorably discharge, and punish American service members for violations of the laws of war. The Abu Ghraib prosecutions, whatever their inadequacies, demonstrated that the American military justice system can and does hold soldiers accountable for abuse. The Justice Department may prosecute American officials who commit crimes under federal law, including torture, which is a federal crime under 18 U.S.C. § 2340. Congressional oversight, inspector general investigation, the Freedom of Information Act, an independent press, and civil litigation all provide additional accountability mechanisms that collectively constitute a more robust system than secret ICC proceedings.

The proper answer to genuine American misconduct is to strengthen these domestic institutions — to ensure that military justice proceedings are sufficiently independent, that inspector general offices are adequately resourced, that whistleblower protections are robust, and that Congress exercises its oversight function aggressively. These are imperfect mechanisms. The ICC is also imperfect, and additionally suffers from all the democratic legitimacy and structural bias problems identified above. Trading imperfect domestic accountability for imperfect external accountability gains nothing and sacrifices constitutional principle in the process.

Regarding the ICJ specifically, the United States remains fully committed to international dispute resolution through diplomatic negotiation, bilateral arbitration agreements, and the WTO dispute settlement mechanism for trade matters — each of which involves submission to external judgment in carefully defined, consensually negotiated contexts. What the United States should reject is not all external arbitration but the specific model represented by the ICJ's compulsory jurisdiction and the ICC's universal criminal mandate: jurisdiction claimed rather than consented to, exercised by institutions with no accountability to the American democratic process.

Part Six: Sovereignty as a Precondition for International Order

Finally, it must be said plainly: the international order critics claim the United States would damage by rejecting ICC and ICJ jurisdiction is not actually sustained by those courts. It is sustained by American military power, American diplomatic engagement, American economic weight, and American commitment to a rules-based framework that the United States has largely constructed and maintained since 1945.

The ICC has never detained a defendant who did not consent to appear or was not delivered by a willing state. It has no enforcement mechanism independent of major-power cooperation. Its writ does not run against China, Russia, India, or any other great power. It is, functionally, a tool operable against small and middle powers whose leaders lack superpower protection. The pretense that it represents a universal legal order to which all states are accountable is precisely that — a pretense.

The ICJ is similarly dependent on state compliance with its judgments. The United States ignored its 1986 Nicaragua judgment without material consequence. Russia ignored its 2022 order to halt military operations in Ukraine — unsurprisingly, because no enforcement mechanism exists. The notion that these courts constitute the backbone of international order is flatly contradicted by the actual sources of international stability: alliances, deterrence, economic interdependence, and the diplomatic management of great-power competition.

Asserting American sovereignty over American actions and personnel is not a withdrawal from international engagement. It is an honest acknowledgment of where actual international order comes from, and a refusal to accept constraints that apply asymmetrically to democratic nations while authoritarian powers operate freely. A United States genuinely committed to human rights and international law advances those values most effectively by maintaining the credibility, capacity, and freedom of action to enforce them — not by submitting to institutions that constrain American power without meaningfully constraining anyone else.

Conclusion: The Courage to Govern Ourselves

Self-governance is not a privilege extended by international institutions. It is the foundational premise from which all legitimate governmental authority derives. The American people, through their Constitution, their elected representatives, their courts, and their democratic deliberation, retain the sovereign authority to govern American conduct — including American conduct abroad.

The ICC and ICJ represent a genuine philosophical challenge to that premise: a claim that sovereignty must yield to supranational authority as a condition of membership in the international community. That claim should be rejected — not grudgingly, not temporarily, not as mere tactical positioning, but as a principled constitutional commitment grounded in the deepest understanding of why self-governance matters and what it requires.

The United States should formalize its rejection of both institutions' jurisdiction through clear legislative action, should withdraw any remaining treaty provisions that create ICJ jurisdiction, should actively support the American Servicemembers Protection Act's continued enforcement, and should articulate clearly and consistently to allies and adversaries alike that American personnel and American policy decisions are accountable to American law and American democratic institutions alone.

To some, this will seem like arrogance. It is not. It is the sober recognition that constitutional democracy is a fragile and precious achievement, that its integrity requires constant vigilance against external erosion, and that no international institutional arrangement — however idealistic its founding purpose — is worth the price of surrendering the consent of the governed as the ultimate source of legitimate legal authority.

The United States should govern itself. That is not a concession to lawlessness. It is the definition of ordered liberty.

The answer, enshrined in our Constitution, sworn to by every official who has served this republic, is equally simple: The American people govern America.

Not appointed judges in The Hague. Not tribunals assembled from nations that may be strategic rivals, human rights violators, or ideological adversaries. Not courts whose legitimacy derives from documents the United States Senate never ratified and the American people never endorsed.

I. THE FOUNDATIONAL PRINCIPLE

Let us begin with first principles.

Democratic legitimacy is not merely procedural decoration. It is the moral foundation of just governance. A law is legitimate not simply because it exists, but because it derives from the consent of those it governs — expressed through elections, through representation, through constitutional structures that can be amended, challenged, and reformed by the people themselves.

Supporters of the ICC present opposition as evidence of arrogance — as if only nations with something to hide would resist its jurisdiction.

The Rome Statute creating the ICC was never ratified by the United States Senate. President Clinton signed it conditionally. President Bush unsigned it — a remarkable but legally defensible act. The reason was not impunity. The reason was that serious, sober legal scholars across the political spectrum identified structural problems that no amount of goodwill could paper over.

Consider:

First, the problem of complementarity in practice. The ICC's formal principle is that it only acts when national courts fail to act genuinely. This sounds reasonable. But "genuinely" is defined by ICC prosecutors and judges — not by American courts, not by American law, not by standards Americans had any voice in establishing. The ICC can second-guess American military justice, American prosecutorial decisions, American congressional oversight — and substitute its own judgment. That is not complementarity. That is supremacy.

Second, the problem of jurisdiction over non-member states. The ICC has asserted jurisdiction over nationals of non-member states when conduct occurs on the territory of member states. This means American soldiers deployed in coalition operations could theoretically face ICC prosecution despite the United States never accepting ICC authority. This is jurisdictional imperialism — extending legal reach through the back door of geography when the front door of treaty ratification was never opened.

Third, the problem of politicized prosecution. The ICC prosecutor has significant independent discretion. That discretion has been exercised in ways that raise legitimate questions about selective enforcement. Powerful actors with political motivations can push ICC investigations toward geopolitical ends. We have seen investigations pursued or threatened against American military and intelligence personnel. Whatever one thinks of specific American actions, the appropriate forum for accountability is American courts, American Congress, and ultimately the American voter — not a prosecutor in The Hague operating under pressures neither transparent nor democratically accountable to Americans.

Fourth, the constitutional problem. The Fifth and Sixth Amendments guarantee Americans the right to grand jury indictment, speedy trial, jury of peers, and confrontation of witnesses. ICC procedures do not replicate these protections. Subjecting Americans to ICC jurisdiction means subjecting them to trial under procedures their Constitution explicitly does not sanction. No executive agreement, no presidential signature, no foreign treaty can override constitutional guarantees. This is the Supremacy Clause working as intended — protecting individual rights from being bargained away by governments.

III. THE ICJ: IMPORTANT BUT BOUNDED

The International Court of Justice presents a more nuanced picture, and intellectual honesty requires acknowledging it.

The 1984 Nicaragua case stands as the clearest cautionary example. That withdrawal was not lawless. It was a reasonable response by a sovereign state to a judicial process it concluded had exceeded legitimate bounds.

The Avena case — where the ICJ ruled on consular notification rights and ordered review of criminal sentences — raised profound questions about whether ICJ judgments can directly bind American state courts, overriding American domestic legal processes. The Supreme Court ultimately concluded they cannot, absent congressional action. This was correct. Treaties and international judgments do not self-execute into binding domestic law without democratic sanction.

The United States should engage with the ICJ selectively, on terms it has clearly and specifically accepted, in forums with defined and limited scope. What it should not accept is open-ended compulsory jurisdiction that transforms American foreign policy decisions into subject matter for foreign judicial review.

Here the critics will object: "Without international accountability, what prevents powerful nations from committing atrocities with impunity?"

After more than two decades and billions in funding, the ICC has secured a handful of convictions, almost entirely of African defendants, while serious alleged violations by Russian, Chinese, and other powerful-state actors have proceeded without meaningful ICC consequence. If the measure of accountability is actual results, the ICC's record is modest at best.

Second, American accountability mechanisms are robust and real. The American military justice system has prosecuted war crimes. Abu Ghraib resulted in prosecutions. American courts have adjudicated cases involving government misconduct. Congressional oversight — however imperfect — can investigate, defund, legislate, and expose. The press, civil society, and American voters exert continuous pressure. These mechanisms are imperfect. No accountability system is perfect. But they are democratically grounded, constitutionally bounded, and genuinely operative.

Third, and most importantly: the logic of accountability cannot be limitless without destroying constitutional self-governance. Every argument for expanding ICC jurisdiction is also an argument for reducing democratic control over a nation's most consequential decisions — decisions about war, peace, military force, and national security. A free people must retain ultimate authority over those decisions and ultimate responsibility for accountability when things go wrong. Delegating that accountability to institutions outside democratic control does not enhance justice — it displaces it.

V. WHAT WE SHOULD DO INSTEAD

Rejecting ICC and ICJ compulsory jurisdiction does not mean rejecting international law. It does not mean rejecting cooperation. It does not mean the United States claims a license to do whatever it wishes.

It means:

We support international law through bilateral agreements with defined terms, ratified through constitutional processes, subject to democratic amendment.

We support international accountability through institutions with genuine democratic legitimacy — reformed, with accountable prosecutors, representative participation, and procedural protections consistent with rule of law principles.

We maintain our own accountability mechanisms vigorously and visibly, so that American conduct is genuinely reviewed by American institutions answerable to Americans.

We engage diplomatically with allies and adversaries alike on standards of conduct, making the case for human rights and rule of law through persuasion and example rather than submitting to external compulsion.

We lead by the quality of our actions and institutions, not by subjecting ourselves to tribunals whose legitimacy, independence, and procedural fairness remain genuinely contested.

The erosion of democratic sovereignty is rarely dramatic. It happens gradually, incrementally, through processes that sound reasonable in isolation — each step small, each expansion modest, each new jurisdiction framed as necessary and obvious.

The question of whether Americans are governed by American constitutional processes or by external institutions they did not meaningfully consent to is not a small question. It is the foundational question of political legitimacy.

For 248 years, Americans have fought, argued, amended, and reformed their system of self-governance. It is deeply imperfect. It has produced historic injustices alongside historic achievements. The answer to American injustice is more American democracy, more vigorous American accountability, more engaged American citizenship.

It is not the surrender of American self-governance to institutions that, however well-intentioned some of their architects may have been, do not answer to the American people.

We believe in international cooperation founded on genuine consent.

We believe in accountability rooted in democratic legitimacy.

We believe that American soldiers, officials, and citizens are entitled to the full protections of the Constitution under which they serve.

And we believe that the American people — not judges in The Hague — are the ultimate sovereigns of this republic.
